## Introduction

In these exercises, you'll practice mostly with writing Markdown
and organizing and documenting a research project.

You'll write a separate file for each exercise,
which should all go in a folder `week02/exercises` inside your personal dir
at `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Solutions for most questions are at the [bottom of this page](#solutions) ---
but do give each question a genuine try before looking!
:::

### Setting up

Start a VS Code (`Code Server`) session at OSC OnDemand,
as we did in class and as described in
[the VS Code lecture](./w2c_vscode.qmd#starting-vs-code-at-osc).
Make sure the Working Directory is your personal dir,
`/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/<user>`.

1. In the VS Code file explorer, you should see the `week02` and `week03` folders
   you created in class. Hover your mouse over the `week02` folder:

   Click the "New Folder..." icon

## Exercise 2: Writing a Markdown document

In this exercise, you'll build a Markdown document from scratch.
The idea is to practice the syntax,
so don't spend a lot of time thinking about the content.

1. Create a file `2_writing-markdown.md` in your `week02/exercises` folder.

2. Open a preview of the Markdown document to the side.
   Keep an eye on the preview after every step below.

3. On the first line, add a level-1 header with the document's title:
   `Markdown practice`.

4. Add a level-2 header `Course tools`,
   and below it a paragraph of two sentences about the tools you've used
   so far in this course.

5. Below that paragraph, add a bulleted list with three tools.
   For each item, put the name of the tool in **bold**,
   followed by a dash and a few words about what it's used for.

6. Add a level-2 header `Starting a VS Code session at OSC`,
   and below it a numbered list of steps to start a VS Code session.

7. Add a level-2 header `Useful links` with a bulleted list of three links
   to the OSC websites we discussed (links can show or hide the URL --- as you wish).

8. Add a level-2 header `A quote`,
   and below it a blockquote with one sentence that you found interesting from
   this week's reading [@markowetz2015].
   Below the blockquote, in a regular paragraph, say where the quote is from.

9. Add a level-2 header `Code`, and below it:

   - A sentence that mentions the file name `README.md`,
     formatted as inline code.
   - A code block with `bash` syntax highlighting containing these two lines:

     ```bash
     # Print the current date and time
     date
     ```

10. Add a horizontal rule, followed by a level-2 header `To do`
    and a bulleted list of two things you want to practice more.

11. In the OnDemand file browser, use the `Upload` button to upload an image
    from your own computer into your `week02/exercises` folder.
    Then embed it in `2_writing-markdown.md` with a caption,
    and check that it shows up in the preview.

12. Browse the [Markdown Guide's cheat sheet](https://www.markdownguide.org/cheat-sheet/),
    find one syntax element that we didn't cover in class, and try it out in your document.

## Exercise 4: A project folder

In this exercise, you'll build the skeleton of a research project folder,
with placeholder files and a `README.md`.
**Start by picking one of the two project options below.**

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Option A: Your own project

Use a research project of your own;
either one you are working on now, or one you expect to start soon.

Only pick this option if you can name about ten files that the project
has or will have, and can say several things about its data:
where it came from, when, and from whom.

Since this is just for practice,
it's fine if you make up some placeholder/dummy file names and details,
but if you feel like you'd have to make up too much, use Option B instead.

### Option B: A fictional RNA-seq project

You are studying how drought stress affects gene expression in maize
(_Zea mays_).

You grew 24 plants (12 well-watered "control" plants and 12 drought-treated plants)
and harvested leaf tissue from each plant.
The CFAES Molecular Biology and Genomics Core prepared and sequenced
the RNA-seq libraries,
and you downloaded the raw sequence data from them on May 1, 2026.
The next day, you downloaded the maize reference genome
(assembly `GCF_902167145.1`) from NCBI.

These are the files you have so far:

- `SampleSheet Final.xlsx` --- the spreadsheet from the sequencing facility
  with sample IDs, treatments, and harvest dates
- `ctrl01_R1.fastq.gz` and `ctrl01_R2.fastq.gz` --- raw reads for control plant 1
- `drought10_R1.fastq.gz` and `drought10_R2.fastq.gz` --- raw reads for
  drought-treated plant 10
- `GCF_902167145.1_genomic.fna` --- the reference genome you downloaded
- `01_align-reads.sh` --- a script that aligns the reads to the reference genome
- `counts.csv` --- the gene count table produced by that script
- `02_plot-counts.R` --- a script that makes figures from the count table
- `Fig 1 FINAL v3.png` --- a PCA plot of all samples, made by that script
- `diary.md` --- your lab notebook, with an entry for each day you worked
  on the project

Final notes:

- _You also have the reads for the other 22 plants, but there is no need to list all of those._
- _Most of these names are already fine: _only two of them need to be changed._
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Now, whichever project you picked:

1. Within your `week02/exercises` folder, create a folder for the project.

2. Inside it, create the top-level subfolders you would use.
   For example, `data`, `scripts`, `results`, and `doc`,
   but you're free to use a different (consistent!) set of names.

3. Add any subfolders you need, such as `data/raw` and `data/meta`.

4. Create an **empty placeholder file** for each of the project's files,
   in the folder where it belongs and with a name that follows the file
   naming rules:

   - _Option A_ --- use about ten files that your project has or will have.
   - _Option B_ --- use the file list above,
     fixing the two file names that don't follow the rules.

5. In the top level of your project folder, create a `README.md` with:

   - A level-1 header with the project name
   - A paragraph describing what the project is about
   - A level-2 section `Folder structure` with a list of your folders,
     each with a few words about what goes in it.
     Format the folder names as inline code.
   - A level-2 section `Data` describing where the data came from, when, and from whom
   - A level-2 section `Contact` with your name and your email address as a clickable link

6. In your `doc` folder, open (or create) the lab notebook file `diary.md`,
   and add one entry: a level-2 header with a date,
   followed by a couple of sentences about what you did that day.

   - _Option A_ --- use today's date and describe this exercise.
   - _Option B_ --- use `2026-05-03`, the day you ran the alignment script.

7. Check both Markdown files in the preview and fix any formatting problems.

## Solutions

### Exercise 1

<details><summary>The ten problems, and the fixed file.</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The problems were:

1. No space after the `#` of the title, so it isn't a header.
2. No blank line between the paragraph and the list below it.
   VS Code's preview is forgiving and still shows a list here,
   but stricter renderers (including Quarto's, in week 14) will not ---
   so always leave the blank line.
3. No space after the `-` of the second list item, so it isn't a list item and
   is added to the previous one instead, one the same line.
4. The link has its two parts reversed:
   the `[link text]` comes first, and then the `(URL)`.
5. The inline code for `notes.md` has an opening backtick but no closing one,
   so it doesn't show up as inline code in the preview.
6. `**really*` has two asterisks on one side and only one on the other.
   Only one asterisk on each side is used, so you get *italic* instead of
   **bold**, with a leftover (literal) `*` in the output.
7. No blank line before the `## Things to try next week` header.
   Again, VS Code's preview accepts this, but not every renderer will.
8. The `bash`/`date` code block lost its triple backticks,
   so it shows up as regular text and as a single line.
   **Note:** *Within a code block, you do not need blank lines to avoid merging*
   *lines together! Since there are no "paragraphs" in a code block,*
   *the renderer will not merge lines together.*
9. The table is missing the row of dashes below the header row,
   so it isn't rendered as a table, and once again is collapsed into a single line.

Finally, the two sentences "I started a VS Code session at OSC." and
"Then I opened a Markdown file." are on separate lines in the source but end up
in one line in the output: a single line break is ignored.
While notable, this isn't **necessarily** a problem, and you may in fact deliberately
write Markdown with short lines like this, so that the source is easier to read.
But in the solution below, we assumed that the two sentences were meant to be two
paragraphs, and we added a blank line between them.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

And here is the fixed file:

````markdown

The guide is [Markdown Guide](https://www.markdownguide.org).

```
````

### Exercise 3

<details><summary>Better file names.</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Several other answers are possible ---
what matters is that your names are machine-readable, human-readable,
and sort correctly.

1. `sample2_R1.fastq` &rarr; `sample02_R1.fastq`\
   Without a leading zero, `sample10` sorts before `sample2`.
   With 40 samples, two digits are enough.

2. `RNAseq counts FINAL.csv` &rarr; `rnaseq-counts.csv`\
   The spaces are not machine-readable, and capitals are best avoided too.
   While there is some nuance here, you should generally also avoid qualifiers
   like "FINAL" (would the next version be "FINAL**2**"?).
   Instead, be more specific and/or use version control (week 5 of this course).

3. `plot1.png` &rarr; `pca_all-samples.png`\
   The original is machine-readable but not human-readable:
   it says nothing about what the figure shows.

4. `2019_3_7_field_notes.txt` &rarr; `field-notes_2019-03-07.txt`\
   The date needs leading zeros and hyphens to sort correctly,
   and underscores are better reserved for separating units
   (here: the date from the description).

</details>

### Exercise 4

_These solutions use the fictional project of Option B ---_
_but the same reasoning applies to your own project._

<details><summary>**A)** The project folder, with all files in place.</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

```bash-out-solo
maize-drought/
|-- README.md
|-- data/
|   |-- meta/
|   |   |-- samples.tsv
|   |-- raw/
|   |   |-- ctrl01_R1.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- ctrl01_R2.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- drought10_R1.fastq.gz
|   |   |-- drought10_R2.fastq.gz
|   |-- ref/
|   |   |-- GCF_902167145.1_genomic.fna
|-- doc/
|   |-- diary.md
|-- results/
|   |-- counts/
|   |   |-- counts.csv
|   |-- figures/
|   |   |-- pca_all-samples.png
|-- scripts/
|   |-- 01_align-reads.sh
|   |-- 02_plot-counts.R
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

Some things to note about **where the files go**:

- The sample sheet is a form of data so it belongs in `data` rather than in `doc`.
  In omics projects where the omics data is the main source of data,
  we often consider such sample information "metadata", so it can go in `data/meta`.
- `counts.csv` is produced by one of your scripts, which makes it a *result*,
  even though the next script uses it as input.
- The reference genome is data that you downloaded rather than generated,
  so it goes in `data` too.
  But in its own subfolder, since it is not data *about* your samples.
- The lab notebook is documentation, so `diary.md` goes in `doc`.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

And about the **two files that had to be renamed**:

- `SampleSheet Final.xlsx` &rarr; `samples.tsv`\
  The spaces and capitals make it hard to work with,
  "Final" says nothing about the content,
  and the file should be converted from Excel to a plain-text format.
- `Fig 1 FINAL v3.png` &rarr; `pca_all-samples.png`\
  Again spaces and capitals, and the name says nothing about what the
  figure shows.
  Keeping track of versions in the file name is what version control is
  for (week 5).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

The other names were already fine.
Note that the scripts are numbered,
which shows the order in which they should be run,
and that the sample numbers have a leading zero
(`ctrl01` rather than `ctrl1`) so that they will sort correctly.

</details>

<details><summary>**B)** An example `README.md` file.</summary>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

````markdown
# Maize drought RNA-seq

An RNA-seq experiment to test how drought stress affects gene expression in
maize (_Zea mays_).
Leaf tissue was harvested from 24 plants:
12 well-watered controls and 12 drought-treated plants.

## Folder structure

- `data/raw` - raw FASTQ files as received from the sequencing facility
- `data/meta` - metadata about the samples
- `data/ref` - the maize reference genome
- `scripts` - all scripts, numbered in the order in which they are run
- `results` - output of the scripts: count tables and figures
- `doc` - project documentation, including the lab notebook `diary.md`

## Data

- The raw RNA-seq reads were produced by the CFAES Molecular Biology and
  Genomics Core and downloaded on 2026-05-01.
  Their sample sheet is in `data/meta/samples.tsv`,
  converted from the original Excel file.
- The maize reference genome (assembly `GCF_902167145.1`)
  was downloaded from NCBI on 2026-05-02.

## Contact

Jane Doe - [doe.1234@osu.edu](mailto:doe.1234@osu.edu)
````

</details>
